summary: Expands destination-based remote triggered black hole filtering, a technique to mitigate denial-of-service attacks, by combining it with unicast Reverse Path Forwarding so traffic can also be filtered by source address. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a bully keeps sending junk, you can tell the doorman to drop anything from a certain address. This improves how that is done.

questions: what is remote triggered black hole filtering
source based vs destination based filtering
subtitle: Defending networks from denial-of-service attacks by routing bad traffic to /dev/null.

tldr.problem: Denial-of-service attacks can flood network links with traffic destined to a victim, using up bandwidth and causing collateral damage.
tldr.mechanism: Remote Triggered Black Hole filtering uses BGP to announce discard routes for target addresses, dropping attack traffic at the network edge. Adding unicast Reverse Path Forwarding allows filtering by source address too.
tldr.outcome: Operators can quickly block attack traffic by announcing BGP routes with a chosen community, filtering at line rate without expensive access control lists.

facts.label: uRPF modes
facts.value: Strict (best path only) and loose (any route)

today: RFC 5635 is an Informational document that remains current. RTBH filtering remains a widely deployed technique for protecting networks from denial-of-service attacks, both for destination-based and source-based filtering.

sections.title: Denial-of-Service Attacks and RTBH
sections.content:
Network operators face denial-of-service attacks where attacker traffic destined to a victim overwhelms network links. While access control lists can filter traffic, routers can forward packets much faster than they can filter, and they support many more forwarding table entries than filter entries. Remote Triggered Black Hole (RTBH) filtering solves this by leveraging BGP and the forwarding table to drop attack traffic at line rate.

When a customer is under attack, the service provider can use RTBH to announce a BGP route for the target address, pointing to a null (discard) interface. Participating routers install this route in their forwarding table, causing attack traffic to the target to be dropped at the edge of the network. This prevents collateral damage to other systems and preserves network resources, though the target itself becomes unreachable. Additionally, this RFC expands RTBH to filter by source address, allowing operators to block traffic from specific attack origins.
sections.plainLanguage: When lots of junk mail is coming to your house, instead of filtering every piece, you tell the post office to throw it all away before it gets to your street.

sections.title: Destination-Based Black Hole Filtering
sections.content:
Destination-based RTBH filtering involves five configuration steps:

Step 1: Discard Address Schema. An address is chosen as the discard address, often from TEST-NET (192.0.2.0/24) or RFC 1918 space. Multiple addresses can be used for different incidents: 192.0.2.1 for incident 1, 192.0.2.2 for incident 2, etc. This allows operators to monitor drop counts per incident.

Step 2: Discard Routes. A static route pointing to the discard address is installed on edge and perimeter routers, with the destination interface set to null or discard.

Step 3: BGP Policy. A BGP policy on routers with the discard route sets the next-hop to the discard address for routes announced with a chosen BGP community. Policies typically accept only specific /32 prefixes to avoid accidentally blocking larger address ranges.

Step 4: Egress Filters. Safety filters are configured to prevent the triggering BGP announcements from leaking outside the network. These filter by prefix length and deny the RTBH communities.

Step 5: Trigger Router. A trigger router or management system is configured to announce the target address via iBGP with the RTBH community and NO_EXPORT, allowing the operator to quickly activate and deactivate filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: First, pick a dummy address in the post office. Second, tell edge routers where to throw discarded mail. Third, set up BGP rules to treat announced target addresses as going to the dummy address. Fourth, add safety filters so mistakes don't leak out. Fifth, set up a command center to turn filtering on and off.

sections.title: Source-Based Filtering with Unicast RPF
sections.content:
When attacks originate from botnets configured to follow DNS (re-resolving the target domain and adapting to address changes), source-based filtering becomes valuable. Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) enables this: the router performs a route lookup on the packet's source address and checks if the packet arrived on a valid interface for that source.

In strict mode, the router checks if the ingress interface is the best path back to the source. Asymmetric routing can cause legitimate traffic to be dropped. In loose mode, the router simply verifies that any route to the source address exists, which is more permissive but still blocks spoofed traffic.

To deploy source-based RTBH with uRPF, the same five steps as destination-based RTBH are followed, with the additional step of enabling uRPF on predetermined interfaces. When a source address needs to be blocked, it is announced with a different BGP community. The uRPF check will fail for packets from that source, and they will be discarded. Unlike destination-based filtering, source-based RTBH announcements must not be accepted from outside the local network and ideally only from internal attack mitigation systems.
sections.plainLanguage: With source filtering, the mail carrier checks if the sender's address is real before delivering. If the sender looks fake or is on your blocklist, the mail gets thrown away.

sections.title: Flexibility and Advanced Configurations
sections.content:
RTBH filtering supports several advanced deployment patterns. Multiple Discard Addresses allow different incidents to be tracked separately, enabling operators to monitor how much traffic is being dropped for each attack. Multiple Trigger Communities can divide the network into sections (peering routers, customers, data centers) so filtering can be applied to specific parts of the network, useful for troubleshooting or isolating the source of attacks.

Customer-Triggered RTBH relaxes policy rules to allow customers to enable filtering for their own prefixes without operator intervention. This requires strict authorization checks to ensure customers only announce prefixes they own. Granularity through Communities can distinguish filtering for all routers, peering edges only, customer networks only, or data centers, allowing operators to understand attack patterns better.

Configuration samples for Cisco and Juniper routers are provided in the RFC. The trigger router can be set up as a route reflector that does not receive any prefixes, allowing a low-cost device to initiate filtering. The key requirement is that adding or removing triggers must be quick and easy, often automated by attack detection and mitigation systems.
sections.plainLanguage: You can block in different parts of your network, let customers block their own stuff, and track attacks separately. A cheap computer can be the control center.

sections.title: Security and Risk Management
sections.content:
RTBH filtering is powerful enough to cause significant traffic loss if misconfigured. Announcements triggering black-holing must be carefully controlled:

No Leakage: All RTBH announcements must carry the NO_EXPORT community to prevent them from being advertised outside the operator's network. Egress prefix filters add a safety layer in case the community marking fails.

Source Validation: RTBH announcements must not be accepted from outside the network, except where customer-triggered filtering is explicitly deployed. When accepting from customers, operators must verify that customers only announce prefixes they are authorized to advertise.

Scope Restrictions: Destination-based RTBH should typically only accept /32 prefixes, preventing accidental blocking of entire networks. Longer prefixes may be needed when many attack targets fall within the same /24, but extreme caution is required to avoid collateral damage.

For source-based filtering, announcements must be generated only internally. Unlike destination filtering, source-based routes should never be propagated externally. This RFC does not introduce new security threats beyond the potential for misconfiguration, but proper policy and careful implementation are essential.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest risk is telling the whole internet to throw away good mail by mistake. So: always mark the orders with no-export, only let authorized people place orders, and start with small blocks to avoid huge mistakes.
